name: The Google Effect
statement: We forget facts we believe we can look up, remembering instead where to find them.
statementAccent: remembering instead where to find them
meaning: The Google effect, also called digital amnesia, is the tendency to forget information that can be readily found online, while better remembering where to find it than the information itself. When people expect to have future access to a fact through a search engine or device, they are less likely to remember the fact and more likely to remember the path to it. Identified by Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu, and Daniel Wegner in a 2011 study in Science, it frames the internet as a form of external, or transactive, memory: a store we offload information to, much as we rely on other people to remember things for us. Suggestive but not fully settled, since some findings have failed to replicate, it is an influential idea about memory in the digital age.
mechanism: The effect rests on transactive memory, Daniel Wegner's concept that people distribute the burden of remembering across external stores, traditionally other people and now the internet, treating them as memory partners. When we believe information will remain accessible, the mind economises by not deeply encoding the content itself and instead encoding where to retrieve it. In the original experiments, participants who expected information to be saved recalled it less well but were better at remembering the folder or location where it was stored, and difficult questions primed thoughts of computers. This is adaptive offloading rather than failing memory: limited cognitive resources are redirected from storing facts toward storing access paths, letting the external store hold the details.

examples.text: In Sparrow, Liu, and Wegner's 2011 study, people who expected information to be saved recalled the information less but remembered better where it was stored.
The study framed the internet as a transactive memory store, an external system we offload facts to, like relying on a friend to remember something for us.
Later studies in 2018 and 2020 struggled to replicate the effect, while a 2024 meta-analysis offered renewed support, so its status is not fully settled.

variants.name: Transactive memory
variants.text: Daniel Wegner's framework of offloading memory to external stores, whether other people or the internet, treating them as partners that hold information for us.

variants.name: Cognitive offloading
variants.text: The broader idea of using external tools, from notes to search engines, to reduce the memory load carried internally, of which the Google effect is one instance.

whyItMatters: The Google effect is an influential idea in the psychology of memory in the digital age, framing search engines and smartphones as external memory stores that change what we bother to remember. It informs debates about whether constant access to information reshapes cognition, education, and expertise, and whether offloading facts to devices frees the mind for higher-order thinking or erodes knowledge. By recasting forgetting as adaptive offloading through transactive memory rather than simple decline, it offers a nuanced view of how humans have always distributed remembering, now extended to the internet. Its contested replication record also makes it a reminder to weigh striking claims about technology and the mind carefully.

limits: The Google effect is suggestive but not fully settled; some of the original findings failed to replicate in 2018 and 2020, though a 2024 meta-analysis offered renewed support, so its robustness is uncertain. Whether human-computer interaction truly counts as transactive memory is itself debated, since some argue computers are tools rather than genuine cognitive partners. The effect is modest, and it reflects adaptive offloading rather than wholesale memory loss, so strong digital-dementia claims overstate it. Its magnitude and boundary conditions, when and for whom people offload versus encode, remain incompletely mapped, so it is a useful framing rather than a fully established law of memory.
misreadings: The Google effect does not mean the internet makes us stupid or destroys memory; it reflects adaptive offloading, shifting resources from storing facts to storing where to find them, an extension of how we have always used external memory. It is about remembering access paths rather than content, not about a general collapse of memory. And it is not firmly settled: replication has been mixed, and the strong digital-dementia narrative is contested and sensationalised relative to the modest effect the research actually describes.
origin: Identified by Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu, and Daniel Wegner in their 2011 Science paper Google Effects on Memory, building on Wegner's transactive-memory concept, with subsequent replication attempts giving mixed results.
